vignette:
Leo describes his studio as the one place he could always breathe. The familiar scent of turpentine and linseed oil was, for years, his signal to relax. Now, he often finds himself just standing in the middle of the room, staring at a blank canvas, the air thick with something he can't name. He's 24, with a talent that feels older than he is, but the hands that once moved with fluid confidence across the canvas now feel foreign to him.

It all started two years ago with Kara. She had loved his work, showing up at his first gallery show and speaking about his use of color with an intensity that made him feel seen for the first time. The relationship was a whirlwind of passion and inspiration. He painted her constantly, fascinated by the way light caught in her dark hair. The first time she got angry, truly angry, was over a misplaced set of palette knives. He'd dismissed her shouting as part of her fiery personality. The first time she threw something, a ceramic mug that shattered against the wall behind his head, he told himself it was a one-time thing, a mistake fueled by stress.

The violence escalated slowly, insidiously. It was never a simple beating; it was more chaotic, more personal. She would grab his wrists while he was trying to work, her grip bruisingly tight, accusing him of caring more about his paintings than about her. During one fight, she'd shoved him backward over a stool, and he'd landed hard, his head cracking against the concrete floor. He remembers the split second of stunned silence, the coppery taste of blood in his mouth, and the look of cold satisfaction on her face before it melted into performative tears and apologies. He stayed for another four months after that, walking on eggshells, learning to read the subtle shifts in her mood like a weather forecast, bracing for a storm.

Leaving was less a decision than a desperate scramble. He packed two bags while she was at work and never went back, abandoning half of his canvases and supplies. For the first year, he poured all his energy into his art, working with a frantic, obsessive focus. He thought he was fine, that he had escaped and was healing.

Then he met Sam. Sam is gentle, quiet, and supportive. He brings Leo tea in the studio and talks about his paintings with a soft reverence that feels like a balm. But the safety of it is, paradoxically, what's unraveling him. A few weeks ago, Sam accidentally knocked a jar of brushes off a table. The clatter of them hitting the floor sent a jolt through Leo's body so violent he flinched back against the wall, his hands flying up to protect his head. He saw Sam's look of bewildered concern, but for a split second, it wasn't Sam standing there. It was Kara, her face contorted in rage. The studio, his sanctuary, suddenly felt like a cage.

Now, he lives in a state of constant, low-grade vigilance. He finds himself scanning Sam's face for the slightest hint of displeasure, his body tensing whenever Sam moves too quickly or raises his voice to call from another room. He apologizes for everything, for things that aren't his fault, just to keep the peace. Intimacy is a minefield. When Sam reaches out to touch his arm in the middle of the night, Leo often wakes with a gasp, his heart hammering against his ribs, the ghost of a different, harsher touch still lingering on his skin.

His work, once his refuge, has become a source of torment. He avoids using deep reds and purples, the colors of bruises. He'll start a piece, feel a flicker of the old inspiration, and then a wave of exhaustion or a sudden, intrusive memory will wash it all away. He tells himself he is safe, that the past is over. But his body keeps the score, and most days, he feels like he is losing.
